{"id": "107:6/q05", "question": "Why place هُمْ before the verbal predicate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q05/p1", "position": "The explicit, fronted pronoun strengthens the assertion that they show off.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate as emphasis."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q06", "question": "Why repeat ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ in this description?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q06/p1", "position": "Repeating the phrase permits a verb to follow a verb instead of coordinating a verb directly with a noun.", "reasons": "Bursawī transmits the explanation of Burhān al-Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q07", "question": "When does visible worship count as ostentation?", "turns_on": "Whether optional status itself defines condemned riyāʾ or the performer's purpose does; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes the former restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q07/p1", "position": "Visibility alone does not make worship ostentatious; the intention to win praise does, while sincere public duties or acts shown to encourage others are acceptable.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī and Bursawī recommend public obligations as Islamic signs that avert suspicion or blame and private voluntary worship as the usual course, except when it encourages imitation. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Nasafī cite Prophetic wording about not concealing obligations, without a grading in al-Nasafī. Ibn Kathīr says sincere work remains sincere if its performer later enjoys being seen; his two-reward report has a strange route, middling Saʿīd b. Bashīr, rare transmission from al-Aʿmash, and a parallel called gharīb by al-Tirmidhī, with other routes mursal. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects that restricting condemned riyāʾ to optional works is unnecessary: publicly fulfilling a duty or setting an example is not plausibly condemned."}, {"id": "107:6/q07/p2", "position": "The condemnation of showing off should be limited to optional worship; required public duties and examples are exempt.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes this restriction to some commentators and rejects the need for it, though she agrees that sincere public obligations and examples are not condemned."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q08", "question": "What incident illustrates suspicion of public ostentation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q08/p1", "position": "An observer saw a man prolong a thanksgiving prostration in a mosque and said it would have been better at home.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī transmit the anecdote as suspicion of ostentation or reputation-seeking; al-Rāzī says embarrassment must not stop voluntary worship."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q09", "question": "What do the transmitted sayings say about sincerity and ostentation?", "turns_on": "The reports address distinct outcomes and cases: mixed intentions, sincere small deeds, subtle danger, punishment, permissible pleasure after sincere prayer, and public duties.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q09/p1", "position": "God accepts only acts wholly for Him and rejects worship shared with another intended recipient.", "reasons": "Tustarī transmits a command to sincere work, rejecting division between God and kinship; al-Māwardī transmits God's saying that work for another associates a partner with Him and is unneeded by Him."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p2", "position": "Sincere intention makes even little work sufficient.", "reasons": "Tustarī reports the Prophet's instruction to Muʿādh."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p3", "position": "Ostentation is extremely hidden, like a black ant on black ground in a dark night.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī report the Prophetic simile; al-Rāzī states no grading. They and Bursawī say avoiding it is difficult except with disciplined sincerity."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p4", "position": "A Hell valley from which Hell seeks refuge four hundred times daily awaits ostentatious reciters, givers, pilgrims and fighters.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits the report from Ibn ʿAbbās, including those going out in God's path."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p5", "position": "God will expose and humiliate one who publicizes deeds for human notice.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits a Prophetic report through ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, and notes another route through an unnamed man via Aḥmad; Ibn al-Mubārak calls a related Abū Hurayra report a good hadith for show-offs."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p6", "position": "A person pleased when his private prayer is seen receives two rewards, for secret and public worship.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls one Abū Hurayra route gharīb, rates Saʿīd ibn Bashīr middling, and notes the rarity of his report from al-Aʿmash; al-Tirmidhī calls another route gharīb and notes mursal alternatives."}, {"id": "107:6/q09/p7", "position": "God's obligatory duties should be openly declared.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and al-Nasafī cite Prophetic wording, including wa-lā ghumma fī farāʾiḍ Allāh; al-Nasafī gives no grading."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q10", "question": "How does showing off relate to heedlessness in prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether sahw names failures of timing or form, loss of prayer's moral purpose, or deliberate private abandonment; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ expressly rejects timing and bodily-distraction readings.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q10/p1", "position": "It is a further defect in prayer alongside neglect of time or attentive performance.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī transmits Qatāda's indifference to prayer, Mujāhid's treating it lightly, Abū al-ʿĀliya's late prayer and incomplete bowing/prostration, and an account lacking hope or fear; al-Ḥasan adds no regret over missed prayer. Al-Rāzī says prayer must be free of missing its time, distraction during it, and ostentation. Ibn Kathīr gives late ʿAṣr without calm or reverence, perhaps for show, alongside the hypocrites of 4:142."}, {"id": "107:6/q10/p2", "position": "Showing off itself reveals neglect of prayer's purpose: conscious worship of God that should shape conduct and care for others.", "reasons": "Sayyid Quṭb says sincere prayer requires presence before God; Iṣlāḥī says it needs pure intention, yields gratitude and spending, and links prayer with spending as two pillars of sharīʿah. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reads ʿan as heedlessness of purpose: standing before God, restraining wrongdoing, humility and care for needy people, citing 90:11–17. She rejects treating forgetfulness, missed prayer or time, fidgeting, or yawning as the point because even punctual worship can feign humility for benefit. Kur'an Yolu stresses inward faith, intention, sincerity and reverence and cites 1:5 and 3:64 for divine unity; Study Quran contrasts 70:23 and 70:34."}, {"id": "107:6/q10/p3", "position": "Their heedlessness is deliberately abandoning prayer in private while corrupting its inward quality in public.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī contrasts material abandonment with inner corruption; Ibn ʿĀshūr says sahw literally is inadvertent forgetfulness but here sarcastically denotes deliberate neglect, paralleling 'forgetting' associates and heedlessness of signs in al-Aʿrāf and Yūnus; genuine forgetfulness is excused."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q11", "question": "What does the warning teach about showing off, sincere worship and faith?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish the religious gravity of ostentation from whether every person displaying one trait can be identified as a denier or hypocrite.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q11/p1", "position": "Ostentation corrupts devotion and resembles association of partners with God; true prayer requires sincerity.", "reasons": "Tustarī calls it hidden shirk of conduct, distinguishing it from unforgivable shirk concerning God's essence; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī call it a branch of unbelief. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says prayer for people is not accepted. Iṣlāḥī says another motive defeats prayer's purpose; Kur'an Yolu connects sincerity to tawḥīd."}, {"id": "107:6/q11/p2", "position": "The vices expose denial of judgment and call believers to avoid such traits, though an individual Muslim's lapse does not necessarily prove unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says denial of resurrection and recompense is the root of contempt for sacred matters and these vices; he cites Ibn al-Zubayr's caution that Muslims may display them. Al-Rāzī frames the severe threat as a problem because these three sins alone do not make a Muslim a hypocrite. Sayyid Quṭb says religious life joins inner worship and social care and yields cooperation and mercy."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q12", "question": "How does this clause connect to the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "How the consequential fāʾ and descriptive clauses attach the worshippers to the earlier denier, especially if the orphan-pusher is taken as a particular person.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q12/p1", "position": "It continues the warning to inattentive worshippers and joins ostentation to withholding aid.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī joins the clauses to the preceding woe; Sayyid Quṭb identifies the careless worshippers by both later traits. Corpus Coranicum says the emphatic woe opens a vice catalogue and verses 4–6 target ritual neglect; its cross-correspondence sets religious omissions in verses 1 and 4–6 against social omissions in verses 2–3 and 7. Iṣlāḥī treats ostentation and miserliness as causes of devotionless prayer."}, {"id": "107:6/q12/p2", "position": "The consequential fāʾ escalates from denial and orphan-abuse to prayer-neglect, ostentation and withholding, identifying one group of deniers.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says prayer is religion's pillar, ostentation a branch of unbelief and zakāt its bridge; al-Ālūsī adds customary loans. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the causal fāʾ makes show-praying hypocrites part of the deniers; al-Ālūsī transmits a causal reading from prior coordination attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Mālik. Al-Zamakhsharī's syntax, reported by Abū Ḥayyān, joins fa-dhālika to the denier, elides the answer to araʾayta, and treats the woe'

s descriptive plural as standing for a generic singular pronoun."}, {"id": "107:6/q12/p3", "position": "The later vices can form a prompted digression if the orphan-pusher is one named person.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the Kashf author's objection that later prayer-neglect and ostentation would ill fit as further labels of a named orphan-pusher; al-Ālūsī treats denial of religion as the sūra's principal concern and compares a rebuke at 5:91."}, {"id": "107:6/q12/p4", "position": "Calling them 'those who pray' instead of using a pronoun exposes bad treatment of God and people.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī identifies this as the effect of the overt descriptive phrase."}, {"id": "107:6/q12/p5", "position": "The final ostentation and withholding show that even lesser visible good does not overcome their greed.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says they can show off with some smaller good yet cannot give even a trivial benefit; he adds that the best people most benefit God's dependents."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q13", "question": "How does the clause connect with other Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "The sources draw different intertextual links rather than disagreeing over one exclusive parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q13/p1", "position": "The hypocrites' displayed prayer recalls 4:142 and other passages on hypocrisy or ostentation.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Study Quran cite 4:142; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ lists 2:264, 4:38, 4:142 and 8:47; Abū Ḥayyān points back to his treatment of 2:264. Study Quran directs readers to 63:1–8 on hypocrisy; al-Qurṭubī directs them to 2:271 on disclosed charity."}, {"id": "107:6/q13/p2", "position": "True faith's established prayer and spending in 8:4 counter this sūra's showy prayer and refusal to give.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes the prayer-and-giving connection explicit."}, {"id": "107:6/q13/p3", "position": "Al-Kawthar answers the four vices: giving, prayer, exclusive devotion and sacrifice counter stinginess, neglect, ostentation and withheld aid.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī and al-Suyūṭī map the four oppositions, citing 108:1–2; Elmalılı sees al-Kawthar as condensing prior sūras, especially from al-Ḍuḥā, in an account of Muḥammad's rank."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q14", "question": "Is there a comparison outside the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q14/p1", "position": "Matthew 6:5 likewise depicts hypocrites praying publicly to be seen.", "reasons": "Rudolph draws the comparison in Corpus Coranicum."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q15", "question": "What revelation setting is assigned to this verse's sūra or final section?", "turns_on": "Whether references to hypocrisy require a Medinan setting and whether evidence supports a later ending; Asad rejects the split date.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q15/p1", "position": "The whole seven-verse sūra is Meccan, possibly early in the mission after al-Takāthur.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima and Qatāda; Asad dates it to the early mission, probably after sūra 102, and rejects a Medinan final section for lack of historical or textual evidence. Study Quran reports this as the majority view; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows it."}, {"id": "107:6/q15/p2", "position": "The whole sūra is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Wāqidī. Sayyid Quṭb leans to this because hypocrisy and ostentation were unfamiliar in Mecca; Study Quran allows it because political advantage made hypocrisy possible in Medina."}, {"id": "107:6/q15/p3", "position": "The first section is Meccan and the section from 'woe to those who pray' onward is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Burhān attribute this to Muqātil; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran report a split view. Sayyid Quṭb allows later verses appended for thematic continuity, while Asad disputes the Medinan ending."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q16", "question": "About whom were the last three verses reportedly revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q16/p1", "position": "They were revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr quotes Hibat Allāh ibn Salāma's al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh; the plural describes one person as the people of Noah are said to deny the messengers, meaning their messenger."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q17", "question": "What reports discuss reciting this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q17/p1", "position": "A report says recitation brings God's forgiveness to a person who pays zakāt.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī transmits this through Ubayy and supplies no grading."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q18", "question": "How is the sūra's composition used to relate this warning to later events?", "turns_on": "Al-Biqāʿī uses either the sūra's twenty-five words or those words plus the basmala to generate different dates.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q18/p1", "position": "Its twenty-five words point to year twelve AH and Abu Bakr's defeat of apostates and zakāt-refusers, exposing earlier worship as show.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī counts from the start of prophethood and names Banū Ḥanīfa at Yamāma, al-Nujayr in Kinda and al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī in Ṣanʿāʾ as defeated; he says the woe befell showy worshippers invited to pray by their Prophet who turned away."}, {"id": "107:6/q18/p2", "position": "The twenty-five words plus the four-word basmala point to year sixteen AH and the clearing of polytheists, Christians and Magians from the peninsula.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says most converted and others departed to Byzantine lands; he rejects pronoun or letter counts as unnecessary once religion was manifest."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q19", "question": "Does the verse end after يُرَآءُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q19/p1", "position": "In Damascus, Mecca and Medina counts it does not end here; verses 6–7 can form one unit and yield two symmetrical triads.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites Neuwirth's formal comparison with the short woe and longer vice catalogue in 83:1–3; it acknowledges the rhyme potential at yurāʾūn."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q20", "question": "What inward reading is given to showing off?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q20/p1", "position": "The person is veiled from God by creatures or attributes deeds and spiritual states to the dark ego.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes the creaturely veil; Bursawī gives the ego attribution."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q21", "question": "How does the sūra's opening frame the later warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the later vices intensify the opening rebuke or describe a separately appended but joined passage.", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q21/p1", "position": "After recounting favors to Quraysh, the sūra marvels at their denial despite security and provision.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī relates the opening to their denial of the Prophet and his prophethood."}, {"id": "107:6/q21/p2", "position": "The later neglect, ostentation and withholding make religious pretenders more blameworthy than open deniers who mistreat the needy.", "reasons": "Elmalılı contrasts the groups' conduct."}, {"id": "107:6/q21/p3", "position": "Even where final verses are later revelation, their wording is shaped to fit the earlier sūra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the consequential fāʾ as a clue to such a joining."}]}
{"id": "107:6/q22", "question": "Which act do the cited authorities say they show off through?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:6/q22/p1", "position": "They show off through their prayers.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib gives this explanation in reports preserved by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Suyūṭī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q01", "question": "What do the verb and its omitted recipient suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q01/p1", "position": "The missing recipient generalizes refusal to everyone, while the imperfect verb suggests repeated behavior.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says people or petitioners are understood; al-Biqāʿī says no rank is exempt, and the imperfect marks a repeated habit."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q02", "question": "What does al-māʿūn mean?", "turns_on": "Whether māʿūn is a general benefit, a particular due such as zakāt, loaned goods, a regional lexical sense, or a named necessity; the reported authorities, dialect usage, poetry, and unqualified wording supply the grounds.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q02/p1", "position": "Obligatory alms, especially zakāt.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan and many others transmit this gloss. Al-Rāʿī's poem pairs withholding māʿūn with neglect of tahlīl. Al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr appeal to its place after prayer; Ubayy's recitation report conditions forgiveness on payment of zakāt. Quṭrub and later authors explain the name as a small part of much wealth."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p2", "position": "Ordinary household items lent for use.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd and Companions name axe, bucket, cooking pot; other lists include scales, sieve, needle, fire striker, scissors, oven use, and brief storage. Ibn Kathīr stresses that owners retain and recover such items. Reports through Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others concur. Reports also list metal and stone vessels, iron tools, water, salt, fire, and leaven; Ibn Kathīr questions one delegation report's Prophetic attribution."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p3", "position": "All useful benefit, help, generosity, or recognized good.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī treats benefit as the root sense and cites al-Aʿshā and rainwater; al-Zajjāj and Abū ʿUbayda say pre-Islamic use covered gifts and utility, large or small. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Kalbī include customary good deeds. Ibn Kathīr cites every recognized good deed as charity."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p4", "position": "Water, especially rainwater or flowing water.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites Arab usage and a poem of a cloud pouring māʿūn; al-Aʿshā's line is also cited. Al-Rāzī notes that water is precious in scarcity and invokes 7:50 and 76:21."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p5", "position": "Wealth or property in Quraysh usage, or in Aby

ssinian usage.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī give Quraysh's dialect; Sahl al-Tustarī and Abū al-Layth report Abyssinian wealth."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p6", "position": "Water, fire, and salt: essential goods one may not withhold.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha's report names the three; some routes add a needle and leaven. The Prophet's reported answer promises reward for sharing cooking fuel, salt, and scarce water; al-Qurṭubī judges its chain weak."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p7", "position": "Both required alms and small loaned goods, as instances of useful aid.", "reasons": "ʿAlī and ʿIkrima combine them; al-Ṭabarī prefers the inclusive reading because the wording gives no restriction. Ibn Kathīr says the views converge on refusing help by wealth or service; al-Biqāʿī emphasizes due rights and small articles."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p8", "position": "Obedience or willing compliance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and lexicographers report this sense; Abū ʿUbayda's camel anecdote and an Arab rajaz about a compliant camel illustrate it. Al-Rāʿī's poem is taken to couple obedience and zakāt."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p9", "position": "A due right, including the needy person's share of wealth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar insists on the withheld due, although another report accepts Ibn Masʿūd's mutual help as the same point."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p10", "position": "Water and pasture together.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit this paired gloss."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p11", "position": "Easy assistance requiring little effort.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this possibility; al-Qurṭubī says the small act is treated as burdensome."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p12", "position": "Every easy act of obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī prefers this most inclusive sense because it is most beneficial."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p13", "position": "Shelter for someone seeking refuge.", "reasons": "Geiger derives the term from Hebrew māʿôn, dwelling or refuge; Nöldeke accepts the derivation but rejects carrying the Hebrew meaning into Arabic."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p14", "position": "Fire alone.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān enumerates fire as an independent reported interpretation."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p15", "position": "Pasture alone.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān enumerates pasture as an independent reported interpretation."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p16", "position": "A ladle.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān records this specific interpretation."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p17", "position": "Financial assistance or charity before the fixed zakāt levy.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that unspecified charity was obligatory in early Islam before zakāt was instituted."}, {"id": "107:7/q02/p18", "position": "Food or hospitality denied to guests.", "reasons": "The Study Quran records refusal of guests as another interpretation."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q03", "question": "How is the noun māʿūn derived?", "turns_on": "Whether its form is traced to maʿn, maʿūna, a passive of aʿāna, or Hebrew māʿôn; the disputed sound changes and Arabic poetic use are decisive evidence in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q03/p1", "position": "From maʿn, a little thing, on the fāʿūl pattern.", "reasons": "Quṭrub cites an Arab expression for possessing little; zakāt is a small part of much wealth, as are minor gifts and implements."}, {"id": "107:7/q03/p2", "position": "From maʿūna, assistance, with alif replacing the ending.", "reasons": "Al-Jawharī and Abū Ḥayyān report the replacement; al-Samīn prefers it and links it to anything useful."}, {"id": "107:7/q03/p3", "position": "A passive form from aʿāna, to help.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī connects aid to tools and means. Abū Ḥayyān describes metathesis and sound changes; al-Samīn objects to three irregularities and reports a possible answer to the weak-letter objection."}, {"id": "107:7/q03/p4", "position": "A Hebrew loan māʿôn adapted in pre-Qurʾānic Arabic.", "reasons": "Geiger suggests the origin; Nöldeke and Rhodokanakis say the Arabic sense is benefit or gift, possibly influenced by maʿūna, and the Corpus Coranicum allows a deliberate Hebrew echo."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q04", "question": "Why use the words manaʿūn and māʿūn together?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q04/p1", "position": "Their near-anagram and shared sounds sharpen the clash between expected aid and refusal.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls the consonant permutation reversed paronomasia and suggests the rare noun was selected for assonance. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that māʿūn occurs nowhere else in the Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q05", "question": "When is withholding such things forbidden or blameworthy?", "turns_on": "Whether an item is owed, needed for survival, routinely lent, or liable to damage.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q05/p1", "position": "Withholding needed necessities is forbidden; refusal without necessity is blameworthy conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī and Bursevī distinguish need from ordinary requests; the water, fire and salt report supports the duty."}, {"id": "107:7/q05/p2", "position": "Required alms and other established rights must be given.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes the woe concern required rights, including zakāt and surplus water or pasture."}, {"id": "107:7/q05/p3", "position": "Lending ordinary articles was obligatory early in Islam, then became permissible.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports that the emigrants' poverty first made lending obligatory, and changed circumstances relaxed that duty."}, {"id": "107:7/q05/p4", "position": "Refusing to lend to a neighbor who damages the goods incurs no blame.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh gives this qualification in Abū Baṣīr's report."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q06", "question": "Who are the people who withhold?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronouns describe hypocrites or deniers generally, the Quraysh custodians, or one of several named individuals.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q06/p1", "position": "Hypocrites who display prayer but hide their refusal to give.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mālik and Zayd ibn Aslam describe public prayer and concealed withholding; al-Qurṭubī links 4:142 and 9:54."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p2", "position": "The denier of judgment, whose faults can also appear in professing Muslims.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī treats denial as the root of the traits but notes that a Muslim can have a share of them; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls them people professing religion who resemble hypocrites."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p3", "position": "The unworthy custodians of Quraysh.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says their miserliness shows they cannot fulfill the trust they hold."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p4", "position": "A specific man: Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "A report says he drove away an unclothed orphan seeking his own property."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p5", "position": "A specific man: Abū Sufyān.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj says he struck an orphan asking for meat after he slaughtered camels."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p6", "position": "Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports him among the alternative named referents."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p7", "position": "Al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists him as another proposed referent."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p8", "position": "ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾid.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists him as another proposed referent."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p9", "position": "Manāf.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists him as another proposed referent."}, {"id": "107:7/q06/p10", "position": "An unnamed miserly hypocrite.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists this as another proposed referent."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q07", "question": "What events or instructions are reported concerning māʿūn?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted incident or Prophetic instruction is meant, and how the reports are assessed.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q07/p1", "position": "A delegation was instructed by the Prophet to share water, stone cookware, and iron tools.", "reasons": "Reports through Qurra ibn Damʿūs and others give the instruction; Ibn Kathīr calls the Qurra report extremely strange and its Prophetic attribution objectionable because of an unknown narrator."}, {"id": "107:7/q07/p2", "position": "Hypocrites refused Muslims who sought to borrow household goods, and the verse was revealed.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's report specifies buckets, pots and axes."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q08", "question": "Why does withholding bring the passage's warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the woe requires the combined faults, reaches each obligatory default, or censures the character revealed by even a trivial refusal.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q08/p1", "position": "Refusal of even trifling help exposes extreme miserliness and denial of judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī links the conduct to 4:37 and 68:12; Ibn Kathīr infers one who refuses minor loans will also withhold zakāt; al-Biqāʿī traces the vice to denial of recompense."}, {"id": "107:7/q08/p2", "position": "The warning concerns the combined traits of neglected prayer, display, and stinginess.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says denial of a single household item alone does not merit woe; al-Qurṭubī prefers the portrait of hypocrites and cites 4:142 and 9:54. Al-Zamakhsharī calls prayer the pillar of faith, ostentation akin to associating partners, and zakāt its counterpart."}, {"id": "107:7/q08/p3", "position": "Each fault earns a corresponding share of rebuke, especially denial of obligatory aid.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī applies blame to a Muslim with one trait; al-Biqāʿī stresses that the threatened refusal must concern what is due. Al-Rāzī explicitly asks why three faults short of unbelief attract so severe a threat; al-Burhān instead calls withholding every listed item sinful."}, {"id": "107:7/q08/p4", "position": "Failure to help shows prayer lacked sincerity and moral effect.", "reasons": "Quṭb and Iṣlāḥī say genuine prayer should produce generosity and service; 29:45 and 2:177 connect devotion with conduct."}]}

{"id": "107:7/q10", "question": "How do other passages or sūras answer this verse?", "turns_on": "Which neighboring sūra or other Qurʾānic passage is used as a parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q10/p1", "position": "Al-Kawthar answers its failures through generous giving, prayer, devotion and sacrifice.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī, al-Itqān and al-Burhān pair 108:1–2 with refusal of aid, neglect of prayer and ostentation; sacrifice meat is charity."}, {"id": "107:7/q10/p2", "position": "Al-Anfāl parallels prayer, spending, social rights, display and warning.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares 8:4, 8:32, 8:35, 8:36, 8:41 and 8:47, and relates each to a fault in this sūra."}, {"id": "107:7/q10/p3", "position": "Other verses condemn withholding help.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites 68:12 and 70:21; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares hypocrites' clasped hands in 9:67."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q11", "question": "Where and when was the sūra or its closing portion revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether evidence from the setting of hypocrisy locates the entire sūra or only its closing verses in Medina.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q11/p1", "position": "The entire sūra is Meccan, early in the mission.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima and Qatāda are cited; Asad places it probably after sūra 102 and rejects a Medina ending for lack of evidence. Most commentators are also reported to call it Meccan."}, {"id": "107:7/q11/p2", "position": "The entire sūra is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Wāqidī are cited; Quṭb leans this way because political hypocrisy and ostentation suit Medina, and Study Quran allows it. The Study Quran suggests the political advantage of hypocrisy in Medina."}, {"id": "107:7/q11/p3", "position": "Its opening is Meccan and its later verses Medinan.", "reasons": "Muqātil places the move from fa-wayl to the end in Medina; other accounts describe first and second halves. Quṭb allows later thematic attachment. Asad rejects this split for lack of historical or textual evidence."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q12", "question": "What is reported about reciting this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q12/p1", "position": "A reciter who pays zakāt receives forgiveness.", "reasons": "A report through Ubayy or from the Prophet is transmitted without grading by al-Jishumī, al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī; al-Rāzī uses it for the zakāt gloss."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q13", "question": "What titles are reported for this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q13/p1", "position": "It is called al-Māʿūn, al-Dīn, Araʾayta, and al-Takdhīb.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī lists the names and relates them to denial of recompense; al-Itqān gives the first three, and Study Quran says the title comes from the last verse."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q14", "question": "What structural division is proposed for the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q14/p1", "position": "Joining verses 6–7 yields two balanced triads.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum observes a possible rhyme stop at yurāʾūn and two symmetrical triads when the verses are combined."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q15", "question": "What numerical historical allusions are proposed?", "turns_on": "Whether the numerical count includes the basmala and whether any further count is warranted.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q15/p1", "position": "Twenty-five words point to year twelve AH and the defeat of apostates and zakāt refusers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī links the count from the mission's beginning to Abū Bakr's campaigns against Banū Ḥanīfa, al-Nujayr and al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī. He sees the earlier prayer and almsgiving of zakāt refusers as show."}, {"id": "107:7/q15/p2", "position": "The word count plus the basmala points to year sixteen AH and the departure of non-Muslim groups from Arabia.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says many converted and others moved toward Byzantine lands. The basmala adds four words in this reckoning."}, {"id": "107:7/q15/p3", "position": "Further pronoun or letter counts are unnecessary.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says public triumph made the religion manifest without a hidden numerical signal."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q16", "question": "How is the adjacent verb for ostentation read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q16/p1", "position": "Yarāʾūn is also transmitted with shortening and either doubled or undoubled hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records Ibn Isḥāq and al-Ashhab's readings of the preceding verb."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q17", "question": "What inward moral reading is given?", "turns_on": "Whether the refusal is read as total self-withholding or selfish failure of spiritual qualities.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q17/p1", "position": "Withholding wealth and life reflects a failure to give oneself for God's pleasure.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī contrasts it with Abū Bakr, who gave everything and said he left God and His Messenger for himself."}, {"id": "107:7/q17/p2", "position": "Selfishness rooted in lack of love, justice, fear and hope prevents useful aid.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says they withhold money and goods for narrow interests and will not prosper."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q18", "question": "What unusual gloss is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās?", "turns_on": "The transmitted wording and its uncertain referent.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q18/p1", "position": "The owners or intended recipients have not yet come for the items.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr transmit this brief wording from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "107:7/q18/p2", "position": "These people had not yet appeared.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this variant from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "107:7/q18/p3", "position": "What these people brought afterward.", "reasons": "A further al-Durr report uses this unclear wording; its intended referent is not explained."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q19", "question": "How are reports about the items assessed?", "turns_on": "Which report and chain are being assessed.", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q19/p1", "position": "The water, fire and salt report has a weak chain.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says Ibn Mājah records the report cited by al-Thaʿlabī, but judges its chain weak."}, {"id": "107:7/q19/p2", "position": "The household-goods report from Ibn ʿAbbās is authenticated.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says al-Ḥākim authenticated Ibn ʿAbbās's household-goods report, while other scholars transmit related raised reports."}, {"id": "107:7/q19/p3", "position": "The delegation report attributed to the Prophet is objectionable.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls it extremely strange and notes an unknown transmitter."}, {"id": "107:7/q19/p4", "position": "Umm ʿAṭiyya's report has a weak chain.", "reasons": "Al-Durr labels this report weak."}]}
{"id": "107:7/q20", "question": "Why is the unbeliever unnamed when Adam's lapse is named?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "107:7/q20/p1", "position": "Adam's lapse was mentioned after his death and with repentance, to teach later people and honor his rank.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 20:121, says Adam's one lapse and repentance honor him, and cautions that one should not expect Paradise while persisting in greater sin."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q01", "question": "What does tabbat mean?", "turns_on": "Whether tab chiefly denotes destruction, unsuccessful effort, straying, or deprivation of good.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q01/p1", "position": "Ruin or destruction through loss", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and many exegetes gloss loss or ruin; Zamakhshari cites an aged, ruined woman, Razi cites the failed plot in 40:37 and a Bedouin's 'I am ruined' heard by the Prophet, and Ibn Ashur takes the curse as a return of Abu Lahab's own words. Biqai surveys tab, tabab and tibab as loss, deficiency and cutting off: Ibn Maktum, Ibn Durayd and al-Qazzaz distinguish their forms. His extended reversed-root batt survey gives complete cutting, irrevocable acts, old age, weak animals, settled matters, oaths, fasting inten

tion, provision and severed bonds; he also notes unusual senses such as dates, clothing and the chest. Ibn Kathir says Abu Lahab's effort was wasted; Razi connects abandonment of faith, speech and acts with ruin."}, {"id": "111:1/q01/p2", "position": "Frustration or failure of an aim", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says Abu Lahab's previously trusted tribal standing let him repel visitors, but his public hostility made them doubt him; Razi adds his hand on visitors' shoulders. Ata says he expected to overpower Muhammad, so his imagined upper hand failed. Elmalili describes powerlessness and frustration in every effort."}, {"id": "111:1/q01/p3", "position": "Being emptied of all good", "reasons": "Yaman ibn Ri'ab, Ibn Waththab and later transmitters say the hands became empty of every good; Abu Hayyan and Alusi treat this as close to loss and destruction."}, {"id": "111:1/q01/p4", "position": "Going astray", "reasons": "Ata's gloss in Mawardi, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan is 'went astray'; Abu Hayyan calls the varied glosses close in sense."}, {"id": "111:1/q01/p5", "position": "Continuing loss", "reasons": "Al-Raghib, cited by Alusi and Tabataba'i, calls tabab continuing loss; al-Shihab derives it from cutting off. Biqai develops severance as the root that leads to final loss."}, {"id": "111:1/q01/p6", "position": "Destruction rather than ordinary material loss", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati says tab is chiefly destruction, whereas khusr extends to commercial and spiritual loss; she notes tabbat's unique Quranic form and 40:37 as the other root occurrence. Ibn al-Athir supplies an implied verb for tabban laka and Ibn al-Sikkit groups it with grave curses."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q02", "question": "Is the first clause a curse, a statement, or a prediction?", "turns_on": "Whether past tense is imprecation, report, or certain future prediction.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q02/p1", "position": "An imprecation or curse", "reasons": "Farra, Tabari's grammarian, Zamakhshari, Razi, Sibawayh via Burhan, Ibn Kathir, Itqan and Qutb read the first past verb as an imprecation. Ibn Ashur says it replies to Abu Lahab's own insult with fitting requital; Burhan answers Ibn al-Tarawah that it tells the audience Abu Lahab deserves such prayer. Qutb says the curse is issued and fulfilled within the short verse."}, {"id": "111:1/q02/p2", "position": "A factual statement or certain future prediction", "reasons": "Nahhas and Tabrisi allow a declarative reading; Biqai treats the past as already decreed and inescapable, while Islahi calls it a future prediction expressed in certain past tense near Badr. Elmalili says subsequent ruin supports declarative rendering. Islahi rejects reading the phrase as tit-for-tat condemnation."}, {"id": "111:1/q02/p3", "position": "A declarative form that both condemns and effects divine ruin", "reasons": "Elmalili says the informative form can perform a curse and divine ruin, carrying blame; Tabataba'i gives a curse on self and deeds or God's decreed ruin."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q03", "question": "Why is tabbat feminine while tabba is masculine?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q03/p1", "position": "Tabbat agrees with the feminine dual hands; tabba refers to Abu Lahab", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash compares daraba and darabat for the feminine ta and masculine past; Jishumi says tabbat follows the feminine dual hands and tabba the masculine Abu Lahab. Nahhas reports that the still ta can be explained as a particle or a vowel dropped."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q04", "question": "Why open with ruin and repeat the verb?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is invective, emphatic repetition, or a part-to-whole progression.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q04/p1", "position": "Repetition intensifies the curse", "reasons": "Majaz cites 'I saw', 'awla laka' and three plus seven as ten to show Quranic repetition emphasizes. Corpus Coranicum reports Paret's comparison with the double qutila of 74:19-20; Qutb says the opening issues and completes the curse at once."}, {"id": "111:1/q04/p2", "position": "It begins a rebuke like satirical invective", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur likens the destruction opening to 83:1 and Arabic satire: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam and Abu Tammam begin hostile poems with ruin; Abu Bakr ibn al-Khazin adapts the technique for praise. Burhan and Itqan list al-Mutaffifin, al-Humaza and al-Masad as curse openings."}, {"id": "111:1/q04/p3", "position": "Repetition distinguishes hands or work from the whole self", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the joined clause covers the whole man after his harmful hands, a semantic difference sufficient for waw; Biqai calls the completion total and irreversible."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q05", "question": "What do Abu Lahab's two hands refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether hand denotes the person, his acts, resources, paired fortunes, or literal instruments of harm.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q05/p1", "position": "The whole person, by naming a part for the whole", "reasons": "Tabari and Mawardi take 'hands' for their owner; Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Razi and Abu Hayyan call this Arabic part-for-whole usage and cite 22:10 or 2:195. Zamakhshari and Razi cite what hands send ahead; Samin says the wording moves from part to whole. Alusi rejects a proposed restriction that the whole must literally cease with the part and cites established usage. Corpus Coranicum prefers Fischer's synecdoche because the dual fits an abstract 'merits' poorly."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p2", "position": "His deeds or efforts", "reasons": "Tabari takes hands as deeds; Mawardi and Damghani say most action is performed by hands, citing 48:10, 36:35 and 22:10. Muqatil via Wahidi says abandoning faith ruined his hands. Ibn Kathir, Tabataba'i and Alusi see failed efforts against the Prophet; Razi and Baydawi distinguish worthless work from loss of self. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid respectively specify failure in monotheism and good works."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p3", "position": "His literal hands as instruments of harm", "reasons": "Nahhas, Zamakhshari, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur cite a raised stone that God prevented; Tariq's Dhu al-Majaz report says he bloodied Muhammad's legs. Razi cites pushing visitors, blowing on empty hands and a speaking kid goat whose hands he tore; Durr and Alusi recount the hand gesture after the boycott. Ibn Ashur cites al-Nabigha's curse on harmful hands and an Asadi's blessing of helpful hands."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p4", "position": "His wealth and possessions", "reasons": "Thalabi, Mawardi and Baghawi cite the Arabic expression 'little in hand' for little wealth; Abu Muslim contrasts wealth with the self using 39:15. Ibn Atiyya says hands earn, gain and hold property; Study Quran includes possessions."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p5", "position": "His power and means of achieving aims", "reasons": "Razi suggests religion and worldly/future fortune, capacities to gain benefit and repel harm, or weapon and shield. Biqai says both hands represent all human power, giving or withholding and helping or harming; Elmalili sees every worldly and religious means turned against him. Islahi uses an arm-breaking idiom, Fanad al-Zamani's couplet and Ezekiel's Pharaoh imagery for crushing political force."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p6", "position": "A connective idiom like the hand of time", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi and Tabrisi compare the hand of time, year or calamities; Tabrisi and Qurtubi adduce poetry for the idiom."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p7", "position": "His worldly and otherworldly fortunes", "reasons": "Baydawi says the hands can stand for this world and the next; Razi gives religion and worldly or future fortunes, or beginning and end."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p8", "position": "His offspring", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi transmits Mujahid's reading of the ruined hands and ruin as Abu Lahab's children."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p9", "position": "His favors to Muhammad and Quraysh", "reasons": "Al-Maturidi in Alusi reads the two hands as favors Abu Lahab claimed with Muhammad and Quraysh; enmity nullified the first, and Quraysh's defeat the second."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p10", "position": "Failure toward God and toward the Messenger", "reasons": "Razi reports an analysis dividing his failure between not recognizing his Lord's right and not recognizing the Messenger's right."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p11", "position": "His monotheism and good deeds, which failed", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says the hands perished away from monotheism, while Mujahid says they perished away from good works; Mawardi and its full version preserve both."}, {"id": "111:1/q05/p12", "position": "His merits", "reasons": "Rubin, reported by Corpus Coranicum, infers lost merits from a report that Abd al-Uzza vowed to tend al-Uzza's shrine; the same author objects that a dual concrete noun poorly fits abstract merit."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q06", "question": "Who is Abu Lahab in the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether Abu Lahab is the historical uncle or an archetypal figure; accounts also vary his personal name.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet's paternal uncle, Abd al-Uzza son of Abd al-Muttalib", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Baghawi, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur and others identify Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's paternal uncle. {"id": "111:1/q07", "question": "What does Lahab mean and why was he called that?", "turns_on": "Whether the epithet arose from his appearance or resources, or from the sura's fire image.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q07/p1", "position": "Flame or heat, evoking handsome red or radiant cheeks", "reasons": "Bursevi defines lahab as flame or heat. Asad calls the pre-Islamic nickname nonpejorative; Kuran Yolu adds cheeks reddening with anger. Abu al-Duha and Muqatil are cited for the same appearance account."}, {"id": "111:1/q07/p2", "position": "A trait-based kunya marks association rather than an actual son", "reasons": "Zamakhshari compares Abu al-Sharr and Abu al-Khayr and reports the Prophet's calling Abu al-Muhallab Abu Safra for a yellow face. Ibn Ashur says ab can denote association with a thing and cites Taftazani on names as omens and a poem about Abu al-Mahasin; Bursevi says no son Lahab is required."}, {"id": "111:1/q07/p3", "position": "The sura coined or reshaped it to mark a person bound for Hell", "reasons": "Horovitz doubts it was an actual earlier name; Corpus Coranicum sees the later fire image as supplying its meaning, while Tabataba'i and Elmalili stress the final association with Hell."}, {"id": "111:1/q07/p4", "position": "His wealth occasioned the epithet", "reasons": "Bursevi alone mentions wealth as another possible source of the epithet."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q08", "question": "Why does the verse use his kunya?", "turns_on": "Whether public recognition, avoidance of an idolatrous name, honor, humiliation, or fire imagery motivates the kunya.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q08/p1", "position": "It avoids the idolatrous name Abd al-Uzza", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba asks how the Prophet could say a name making someone servant of an idol. Thalabi, Mawardi, Zamakhshari, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Biqai, Itqan and others say Abd al-Uzza was avoided. Mawardi-Full also reports Abd Hashim. Qurtubi calls the idolatrous attribution unfit for Scripture; Itqan says Abu Lahab is the Quran's only kunya."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p2", "position": "It was his best-known designation", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says identifying labels need not describe traits literally and cites people known by kunyas; Mawardi, Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Qurtubi, Tabrisi, Biqai, Alusi and Ibn Ashur say this name was commoner than his given name. Zamakhshari says familiarity makes the hostile identification clear and lasting and compares uninflected Ali ibn Abu Talib and two names distinguished by case; Alusi says it publicizes the curse. Alusi rejects al-Sayyid's claim that fame alone creates the hellish allusion."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p3", "position": "It alludes to his fiery abode", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Qurtubi, Burhan, Nasafi, Alusi, Ibn Ashur, Elmalili and Tabataba'i connect the name with the Fire. Alusi favors an allusion moving from 'one attached to flame' to hellishness and cites al-Miftah that literal and implied senses can coexist; he rejects al-Sayyid's need for prior fame and cites a couplet. Corpus Coranicum notes verse 3 retrospectively brings out the fire imagery."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p4", "position": "It mocks his bright cheeks and pride", "reasons": "Zamakhshari proposes irony directed at his admired cheeks; Razi and Alusi add pride, while Qurtubi says God chose a less flattering fire-name instead of Abu al-Nur or Abu al-Diya."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p5", "position": "A kunya is lower in honor than a personal name", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi say a proper name is nobler than a kunya referring through another; prophets therefore appear by names. Abu Hayyan reports it; Samin objects that this conflicts with calling a kunya more honorable."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p6", "position": "It functions as a fixed personal name without honorific force", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites Abu Amr, Abu Sufyan and other kunyahs functioning as names and says an identifying label is no lie, just as names like Dog or Crow need not describe their owner. Razi says the kunya need not honor; Zamakhshari cites preserved Abu forms in fixed names."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p7", "position": "A kunya respectfully addresses a relative", "reasons": "Islahi treats the title as ordinary Arab respect. Ibn Qutayba says a kunya may imply age and experience, but Qurtubi rejects deriving a general permission to honor unbelievers from this verse."}, {"id": "111:1/q08/p8", "position": "It echoes the later phrase about a fire of flame", "reasons": "Baydawi proposes its phonetic echo of dhat lahab; Alusi says an objection that a pun must fall at the verse ending fails. Corpus Coranicum says verse 3 completes the suggestive name."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q09", "question": "How is Abi Lahab read and explained?", "turns_on": "How the consonant h is vocalized and whether the familiar kunya retains nominative Abu.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q09/p1", "position": "The ha is read with sukun as Lahb", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, and in Qurtubi Mujahid and Humayd read sukūn. Abu Ali compares dialect pairs such as nahr and shamʿ; Abu al-Baqa invokes Kufan analogy. Ibn Ashur adds vowel lightening after an initially vowelled consonant; Abu Shama interprets easing a heavy name and Ibn al-Jazari praises it. Qiraat-Er suggests a shift from flaming act to concrete flame."}, {"id": "111:1/q09/p2", "position": "The ha of Lahab is read with fatha", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir is contrasted with other readers who give fatḥa; Ibn Muhaysin and other names vary by transmitter. Abu Ali treats lahb/lahab as dialect forms and prefers the open hāʾ because 111:3 has it; Baghawi and Abu Hayyan say the later form preserves the verse endings. Abu Hayyan disputes Zamakhshari's Shams Malik analogy."}, {"id": "111:1/q09/p3", "position": "Sukun reflects altered pronunciation of a proper name", "reasons": "Zamakhshari treats the still hāʾ as proper-name alteration and cites Shams ibn Malik; Ibn Jinni and Ibn Ashur compare other transferred proper names and Abu Salma. Abu Hayyan and Samin counter that Shams can be a plural-derived name already bearing that vowel."}, {"id": "111:1/q09/p4", "position": "Abu remains nominative in a familiar uninflected name", "reasons": "Zamakhshari reports yadā Abū Lahab and compares preserved Abu Talib; Razi and Baydawi say a fixed name may keep Abu in nominative. The argument is that changing a famous form could confuse the hearer."}, {"id": "111:1/q09/p5", "position": "Abi is regularly genitive", "reasons": "Nahhas reports Kufan grammarians that yāʾ marks the genitive; another analysis allows a doubly declinable proper name."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q10", "question": "What opposition to the Prophet is reported of Abu Lahab?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q10/p1", "position": "He followed and publicly discredited the Prophet", "reasons": "Tariq al-Muharibi and Rabi'a ibn Abbad report seeing the Prophet invite people at Dhu al-Majaz while his uncle followed, calling him liar or Sabi and warning against abandoning al-Lat and al-Uzza; Tariq adds bleeding legs from stones. Ibn Kathir notes Ahmad's transmission and versions through Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabarani. Wahidi and Qurtubi also preserve the pursuit."}, {"id": "111:1/q10/p2", "position": "He challenged the message through pride and self-interest", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, Mawardi, Razi, Asad and Kuran Yolu connect hostility with rejecting equality and moral judgment; Islahi adds the claim that, as Kaaba treasurer, Abu Lahab diverted funds and defended personal interest while other leaders could have accepted gentler language about idols."}, {"id": "111:1/q10/p3", "position": "He joined Quraysh against his clan and household", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham and Qutb say Abu Lahab and his wife actively opposed him. Qutb describes abandoning Banu Hashim's clan protection, joining the boycott, and ordering his sons to divorce the Prophet's daughters."}, {"id": "111:1/q10/p4", "position": "He funded Quraysh at Badr while staying away", "reasons": "Elmalili says illness kept Abu Lahab from Badr but he paid and sent As ibn Hisham; Islahi says he sent a debtor, perhaps to death. Kuran Yolu notes his material support; Study Quran says he missed the battle."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q11", "question": "How did Abu Lahab die and how was he buried?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on cause of death and burial method.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q11/p1", "position": "A smallpox-like illness and grief killed him after Badr", "reasons": "Elmalili says adasa, like smallpox, struck him and he died seven days after Quraysh lost at Badr. Alusi's account says relatives feared contagion and left the body three days; Kuran Yolu relates grief and a hired burial. Islahi calls it a humiliating death."}, {"id": "111:1/q11/p2", "position": "Hired men buried him in a pit under wood and stones", "reasons": "Elmalili reports hired Sudanese men dug a pit, placed the body with wood and covered it with stones; Kuran Yolu also reports hired Sudanese buriers."}, {"id": "111:1/q11/p3", "position": "A wound inflicted by Umm al-Fadl festered and killed him", "reasons": "Study Quran reports an alternative in which a festering wound from Umm al-Fadl, inflicted in response to his attack on her converted slave, caused death soon after Badr."}, {"id": "111:1/q11/p4", "position": "His corpse was propped by a wall and covered with stones", "reasons": "Elmalili gives a different account: no pit, a body propped against a wall and piled over with stones."}]}
